definition: Cloud robotics is a field of robotics that attempts to invoke cloud technologies such as cloud computing, cloud storage, and other Internet technologies centered on the benefits of converged infrastructure and shared services for robotics.
details: When connected to the cloud, robots can benefit from the powerful computation, storage, and communication resources of a modern data center in the cloud, which can process and share information from various robots or agents (other machines, smart objects, humans, etc.). Humans can also delegate tasks to robots remotely through networks. Cloud computing technologies enable robot systems to be gain capability whilst reducing costs through cloud technologies. Thus, it is possible to build lightweight, low-cost, smarter robots with an intelligent "brain" in the cloud. The "brain" consists of data center, knowledge base, task planners, deep learning, information processing, environment models, communication support, etc.

explainer.lead: Cloud robotics connects robots to remote computing, storage, and communication services instead of making every robot carry all its intelligence onboard. This can make robots lighter and cheaper while letting them share information and tackle more demanding tasks.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a small robot asking a very powerful computer for help, like using a phone to look something up. The robot sends information over the internet, and the computer helps it understand a place or plan a job. Several robots can also share what they learn this way.
tiers.practitioner: A typical setup sends sensor and task data over a network for cloud-based planning, learning, information processing, or storage, then returns results to the robot. This reduces onboard hardware requirements and supports shared knowledge across robots, but makes connectivity and remote infrastructure central design dependencies.
tiers.paperLevel: Cloud robotics denotes robotic systems that invoke cloud computing, cloud storage, and other Internet technologies to use converged infrastructure and shared services. The cloud “brain” may include data centers, knowledge bases, task planners, deep learning, information processing, environment models, and communication support; network connectivity is an inherent dependency.

explainer.example: A lightweight robot sends information about its surroundings to the cloud. A task planner uses that information and an environment model to produce a plan, which is sent back to the robot; the robot avoids carrying all the planning hardware onboard.

explainer.intuition: A robot does not need to carry its entire “brain” with it. By moving demanding computation and shared knowledge into a data center, the same infrastructure can support many robots and other connected agents.
howItWorks: A robot collects information or receives a task and connects to cloud services through a network.
Cloud resources provide computation, storage, environment models, knowledge bases, and task planning.
The cloud can combine information from multiple robots, machines, smart objects, or people.
Plans or processed information return to the robot, while people can also delegate tasks remotely.
explainer.whyItMatters: Sharing data-center resources can reduce robot cost and weight while increasing available computation and storage. It also lets knowledge and information be shared across robots and enables remote human task delegation.
misconceptions: It does not mean every part of a robot is moved into the cloud; the physical robot still senses and acts.
It is not a single product or software platform, but a way of combining robotics with cloud and Internet technologies.
The cloud “brain” is more than storage: it can also include planning, learning, environment models, and communication support.
